News, weighed
not spun.

Every story on Fulcrum ships with the same gauge: how many sources we read, and where each one sits between left and right. You don't have to trust our judgment — you can see the math.

The habit we're not asking you to break

You don't have to quit the nyt.com or Fox tab.

Loyalty to a homepage isn't a character flaw — it's what a reliable habit feels like. Fulcrum isn't a lecture about media literacy. It's a second tab: same story, wider angle, five minutes a day.

A paper of record

Deep, credentialed, slow to correct

Strong newsroom, real sourcing standards — and a house point of view baked into which stories lead and which get buried on page A14.

A cable outlet

Fast, loud, built for outrage

Great at telling you something is happening right now. Less interested in telling you what the other 60% of the country thinks about it.

Fulcrum

Slow news, shown from every side at once

We don't break news first. We wait until a story has coverage across the spectrum, then show you all of it side by side, sources cited.

How a story gets weighed

Same facts. Three ways of framing them.

Each bundle starts with what's actually verified, then shows how coverage tilts left, center, and right — plus what's genuinely still disputed. No single frame is presented as the truth; the facts block is.

3 bundles · sample dataset

BUNDLE 014

Federal minimum wage increase clears committee vote

Verified: A Senate committee advanced a bill raising the federal minimum wage in stages over four years. The vote followed party lines with two crossover votes. The bill next goes to the full chamber; no floor vote date is set.

Left · 9 sources Center · 5 sources Right · 10 sources
24 outlets read
How left-leaning coverage frames it

Emphasizes the gap between current wage and cost of living, and profiles workers it would affect first.

How center coverage frames it

Focuses on procedural odds — committee math, likely floor timeline, and which senators are the real swing votes.

How right-leaning coverage frames it

Leads with small-business cost estimates and warnings from franchise-owner associations about hiring freezes.

Still disputed: the size and speed of any job losses — estimates in circulation range from negligible to significant, and each side is citing a different model's midpoint as if it were consensus.
BUNDLE 015 Blind spot

Federal agency proposes disclosure rule for AI hiring tools

Verified: A federal labor agency opened a comment period on a rule that would require employers to disclose when an AI system screens job applicants. The comment period runs 60 days; the rule is not yet in effect.

Left · 12 sources Center · 3 sources Right · 2 sources
17 outlets read
How left-leaning coverage frames it

Framed as an overdue worker-protection measure, with interviews from applicants who suspect they lost jobs to opaque screening.

How center coverage frames it

Mostly a explainer of what the rule would actually require and which employers it covers — thin coverage overall.

How right-leaning coverage frames it

Barely covered. The little coverage that exists questions the agency's authority to issue the rule at all.

Still disputed: whether this counts as a "blind spot" or just a low-salience story — right-leaning outlets we read simply haven't assigned it much space yet, which is itself the finding.
BUNDLE 016

Border county requests emergency funding for processing backlog

Verified: A county government along the southern border formally requested emergency federal funds to address a backlog at a processing facility. The request cites staffing shortfalls; a federal response has not been announced.

Left · 6 sources Center · 7 sources Right · 13 sources
26 outlets read
How left-leaning coverage frames it

Centers conditions inside the facility and staffing shortages as the root cause, citing county officials directly.

How center coverage frames it

Reports the funding request and the dollar figure, with less emphasis on cause than on what happens if it's denied.

How right-leaning coverage frames it

Places the backlog in the context of overall crossing volume this year, with heavier repetition across outlets.

Still disputed: whether the backlog is a staffing problem, a volume problem, or both — county officials and federal officials have given different primary causes on the record.
NOTE — These three bundles are a worked sample so you can see the format before we show you live ones. Source counts and framing notes are illustrative, not pulled from today's actual coverage. A live edition recomputes every gauge from that day's reporting and links every source it counted.

The transparency ledger

How to check our work.

"Trust us, we're unbiased" is exactly the claim we think you should be skeptical of. So here's what we'd publish if Fulcrum were live — the mechanics, not just the mission statement.

How we'd tag a source's lean

Not one editor's gut call. A standing panel with declared members from across the spectrum rates each outlet on sourcing practice and framing, not conclusions. Ratings are published with dissents attached, and any outlet can formally appeal its tag.

How we'd fund it

Reader subscriptions and a capped, disclosed foundation grant — no advertising, no political donor money, no story ever placed or spiked for a funder. Every funding source above a small threshold would be named on this page, updated quarterly.

What the ranking algorithm does

Nothing. Bundles run in the order coverage crosses the spectrum, oldest first. There's no engagement score, no "you might also like," and nothing tuned to keep you scrolling — we'd rather you finish and close the tab.

Who's in the newsroom

Every editor's byline would link to a disclosed bio, including prior newsroom affiliations. We wouldn't ask anyone their voting history, but we would ask every editor to flag their own blind spots publicly, and hold ourselves to the same disclosure we ask of outlets we rate.

Sample corrections log format
2026-08-11Bundle 014 — reclassified one cited outlet from Center to Right after a source-rating appeal; gauge percentages updated, prior version archived.
2026-08-06Bundle 009 — added a fourth right-leaning source that was missed in initial sweep; "still disputed" note revised.
2026-07-29Site-wide — tightened the definition of "Center" tag after panel review; no bundles required re-tagging.

Starting slow, on purpose

Keep your homepage. Add five minutes.

This isn't a replacement for your morning read. It's what you open right after, to see what your usual source didn't have room for.

STEP 1

Set a starting mix

Use the dial above, or just leave it balanced. You can change it any time — nothing is learned or inferred about you.

STEP 2

Read one bundle

Start with the facts block, then the three frames. Notice which one matches what you already expected — that's the one worth reading last, not first.

STEP 3

Check your blind-spot report

Weekly, Fulcrum would show which bundles you skipped and which side you skipped most — not to shame you, just so it's visible.

This is a concept, not a live product
